s001.text: UPSC, twenty twenty. General Studies Paper One, ten marks, one hundred and fifty words. Discuss the geophysical characteristics of the Circum-Pacific Zone. Here's a catch. Two famous numbers about this zone are quoted everywhere. We could not source either.

s002.text: Read what it asks. Discuss means look at several sides. Geophysical means the physical earth: plates, quakes, volcanoes. So there are four jobs. What and where. The plate setting. The earthquakes. The volcanoes.

s003.text: Start with what it is. A horseshoe of more than four hundred and fifty volcanoes. It runs about forty thousand kilometres around the Pacific. USGS calls it the most active zone on Earth.

s004.text: But why a belt, and not a scatter? Because plates meet there. Fewer than one earthquake in ten falls inside a plate. Along this rim, plates dive under each other.

s005.text: That diving is subduction. The Nazca Plate slides under South America and raises the Andes. It also drags down trenches, eight to ten kilometres deep. The deepest, Challenger Deep, is nearly eleven.

s006.text: The sinking plate carries earthquakes down with it. Foci run from shallow to over three hundred kilometres deep. That sloping line is the Wadati-Benioff zone. And above the hundred-kilometre mark, volcanoes appear.

s007.text: Now we write. One hundred and fifty words, about seven minutes. Open with the horseshoe: the volcano count and the length. Box one fills.

s008.text: Section one is setting and relief. Subduction, with the Andes as the example. Trenches, with a depth. Then two exceptions: the San Andreas fault, and Hawaii's hotspot. Exceptions show you know the rule.

s009.text: Section two is earthquakes. Depth grows along the Wadati-Benioff zone. And seven of the eight biggest quakes since nineteen hundred struck this rim. Add one diagram: a flow from subduction to trench to quakes to volcanoes. Give it a minute.

s010.text: Section three is volcanoes. Arcs rise above the hundred-kilometre mark. And more than half of the world's active volcanoes ring the Pacific. That is USGS's wording, so we use it. Close with the one process, seen four ways.

s011.text: Now the easy answer beside it. It quotes ninety per cent of earthquakes, a share we cannot source. It calls the zone only volcanic. It puts Hawaii on the rim. It blames trenches on faulting. And it adds gravity and heat-flow figures we could not check. Ours leaves them out.

s012.text: Here is the payoff. The same frame answers its cousins. Twenty twenty-one asked about volcanic eruptions and regional impact. Twenty nineteen asked about phreatic eruptions. Learn it once: what, setting, quakes, volcanoes.
